reader.title: Cherokee Strip squatter killings
bases: A cattleman's band of cowboys attacked a small settlement of squatter families over disputed range land, killing the men and burning the cabin or huts (A1, A2, A16).

The first Wichita wire, a separate Chicago Herald special, and Deputy Marshal Wood's account all report three squatters killed by Delaney's cowboys, though they differ on names, date, manner and toll (A1, A2, A16, A17).

summary.text: The Cherokee Strip squatter killings were the killing of three settlers, named in the first reports as Julius Quinn, William Antwerp and Joseph George, by cowboys of the cattleman George H. Delaney in the Cherokee Strip of the Indian Territory in early March 1888.
Wichita dispatches said the men were burned out of their cabin and shot; a deputy U.S. marshal's account added a woman and a cowboy to the dead.
The story ran nationally, and later dispatches reported two cattlemen lynched in reprisal.
According to the first Wichita dispatch, the men had taken up a claim on Rabbit Ear Creek, intending to make entry when the territory opened for settlement.
The land lay in Delaney's range, and he "tried many ways to get the squatters to leave the country, but failed."

In Deputy U.S. Marshal Wood's account, the men and their families had moved from No Man's Land to huts on what they took to be its line, until cowboys said they were inside the Cherokee Strip and ordered them back.
They refused, and the cowboys left after some words.
The first wire, sent from Wichita on March 8, said the three were burned out of a log cabin on Sunday night, March 4, and shot by a mob of cowboys concealed in the underbrush.

A Chicago Herald special added that the cowboys fired the cabin while the men slept and shot their "half-naked victims" as they rushed out; two died on the spot, and the third died after reaching a neighbor's house.
A March 9 dispatch tied to Marshal John Woods likewise described a gang "headed by George Delaney" firing the hut and shooting from the brush.
The marshal's account in the Kansas City Times differed: on Saturday Delaney rode up with about a dozen cowboys and again ordered the families off.
When they refused, "a general shooting followed," killing the three men, Mrs. Antwerp and one cowboy; two women and five children were spared.
In this version the huts were then burned "together with the corpses of the offenders."
Delaney left the area; the Herald special said he was supposed to have gone to New Mexico or Arizona, while the Woods dispatch said he and "a Mexican" came north.
Marshal Wood said he had traced Delaney to Wellington and Winfield and believed he was in Wichita.
The Great Bend paper added that the deputy "does not seem anxious to find him when placed at a disadvantage."
No report of Delaney's arrest, an inquest or a trial appears in the coverage.
The Woods dispatch claimed that "the better class of settlers have already lynched two of the gang," and a Great Bend summary repeated the report.

A March 17 dispatch from Woodward, Indian Territory, reported two cattlemen lynched in the Strip and said farmers, "greatly excited" over the "butchery of three settlers," had organized for protection.
Most papers printed the first Wichita wire, from the Washington Evening Star on March 8 to the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer and St. Paul Daily Globe the next day.
Weeklies and digests in Kentucky, Kansas, Rhode Island and Wisconsin kept it in circulation through late March, often cut to a line or two.

Headlines treated the killings as murder: "Squatters Murdered" in Wheeling, "A Triple Murder" in St. Paul, "Innocent Settlers Murdered" in Phillipsburg, and "An Awful Crime" in the Maysville Evening Bulletin, though the Big Sandy News headed its item "Squatters Squelched."
The Barton County Democrat titled the marshal's version "A Cattle King's Crime."
The Emporia Weekly News, by contrast, ran the same account under the heading "Another Wichita Sensational Special," signaling doubt about dispatches from that city.
None of the reports stated the race of the settlers or of the cowboys.

The men appear as Julius Quinn, William Antwerp and Joseph George in the first wire, Pedro Antwerp and John George in the Herald special, George Burns in the Woods dispatch, and Albert Quinn, John Antwerp and Thomas George in the Kansas City version.
The wire placed the attack on Sunday night, the marshal's account on "last Saturday."
The ambush and shooting-fight versions are both credited to the same marshal, and neither is plainly the better evidence.

accounts.label: First Wichita wire
accounts.gist: Three men were burned out of a log cabin on Rabbit Ear Creek on Sunday night and shot by a mob of cowboys concealed in the underbrush; people nearby charged Delaney's men.

accounts.label: Chicago Herald special
accounts.gist: Delaney's cowboys surrounded the cabin where the men slept, fired it and shot them as they fled; two died there and the third died at a neighbor's after giving the alarm.

accounts.label: Deputy marshal (Kansas City Times version)
accounts.gist: After the families refused orders to move back to No Man's Land, Delaney and about a dozen cowboys came to the huts; a shooting fight killed the three men, Mrs. Antwerp and a cowboy, and the huts were burned with the bodies.

accounts.label: Marshal Woods dispatch (Mar 9)
accounts.gist: A gang headed by Delaney fired the hut and shot the men from the brush; settlers had already lynched two of the gang.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Squatters Murdered', 'An Awful Crime' and 'A Cattle King's Crime' treated the killings as murder by a cattleman's men.
The Emporia Weekly News ran the marshal's version as 'Another Wichita Sensational Special', casting doubt on the Wichita reporting.
Most papers reprinted the first Wichita wire or a one-line digest of it without comment.

Sunday night, March 4 per the wire; Saturday, March 3 per the marshal's account.
No town; a claim on Rabbit Ear Creek, in the Cherokee Strip near the No Man's Land line.
George H. Delaney, cattleman, and his cowboys ('about a dozen' in the marshal's version).
3 (wire) or 5 including Mrs. Antwerp and a cowboy (marshal).
The squatters had refused orders to leave land in Delaney's range.

info: Sunday night, March 4, 1888 (wire); 'last Saturday', March 3 (marshal's account)
A claim on Rabbit Ear Creek in the western Indian Territory (wire); huts in the Cherokee Strip about a quarter mile to a mile east of the No Man's Land line (marshal)

Three men: Julius Quinn, William Antwerp, Joseph George (wire); Julius Quinn, Pedro Antwerp, John George (Herald); Julius Quinn, Pedro Antwerp, George Burns (Woods dispatch); Albert Quinn, John Antwerp, Thomas George, plus Mrs. Antwerp (marshal's Kansas City version); race not stated
Cowboys of cattleman George H. Delaney, with Delaney leading in the marshal's version and the Woods dispatch
Three men killed (wire); three men, Mrs. Antwerp and one cowboy killed, two women and five children spared (marshal)
